strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: localizing the decisive error step in multi-agent LLM trajectories is practically useful for debugging, monitoring, and improving MAS deployments.
The core idea of distilling recurring failure patterns into compact reusable schemata is sensible and potentially valuable, especially given the long-context and low-signal nature of raw MAS logs.
The paper evaluates across several model families and task domains, and includes useful ablations on schema count, cache size, transfer, and stronger schema generators.
The manuscript is generally readable and motivates why naive ICL over full trajectories can fail due to length and noise.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not yet fully convincing. CORRECT-Error is synthetically generated with GPT models, and the same class of LLMs is used to generate injection strategies and schemata; this raises circularity concerns. Human validation only tests whether annotators can distinguish synthetic from human-labeled trajectories, not whether the injected step is truly the unique decisive error under the paper's counterfactual definition.

Data leakage and evaluation protocol details are insufficient. The paper says each trajectory avoids receiving its own schema, but it is unclear whether schemas from closely related test trajectories or the same synthetic generation cluster are available at inference. Masking only the identical trajectory may not prevent near-duplicate leakage in a schema-retrieval benchmark.

Baselines are underdeveloped. The fine-tuning baseline is only lightly specified and appears weak; the paper cites more relevant failure attribution/spectrum-analysis work but does not clearly compare against it. Naive ICL is a useful strawman but not enough to establish state of the art.

Many implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or vague: clustering method and thresholds, schema filtering/distillation rules, cache expansion thresholds, retrieval embeddings and preprocessing, prompt variants, dataset splits, exact sample counts per dataset, and cost/latency measurements. Reliance on proprietary GPT-5 and billions of generation tokens further limits reproducibility.

Claims about efficiency and near-zero overhead are overstated. Offline schema/dataset generation reportedly costs over 3 billion tokens, and online diagnosis still passes long target trajectories plus retrieved schemata to an LLM; no rigorous latency, token-cost, or memory comparison is provided.

Results are mixed on the most credible human-labeled benchmark. Exact-step accuracy remains low on WHO&WHEN, some CORRECT variants show small or negative gains, and much of the strongest performance is on the authors' synthetic benchmark with tolerant Acc@3/Acc@5 metrics.

There are presentation inconsistencies and overclaims, e.g. the oracle comparison text states CORRECT reaches 104% of oracle performance while also describing the oracle as superior, and the algorithm says one schema per cluster but then iterates over each annotated trajectory. These issues make the methodology harder to trust.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately discussed. The paper does not seriously address risks from synthetic benchmark bias, incorrect error attribution, privacy/safety issues in MAS logs, or deployment consequences of confidently localizing the wrong agent/step.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: localizing the earliest decisive error in multi-agent LLM trajectories is practically useful for debugging and reliability.
The core idea of caching compact error schemata rather than retrieving full trajectories is plausible and addresses a real context-length/noise problem with naive in-context learning.
The manuscript attempts a broad empirical evaluation across WHO&WHEN, several task domains, and multiple LLM families, and includes ablations on cache size and number of retrieved schemata.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is not convincing. CORRECT relies on ground-truth annotated trajectories to generate schemas, and evaluation appears to build the schema library from the same benchmark distribution, only masking the exact target trajectory. This leaves substantial leakage and near-duplicate pattern reuse concerns; there is no rigorous held-out application/domain split demonstrating true transfer to unseen MAS deployments.

The new CORRECT-Error benchmark is weakly validated. The human study tests whether annotators can distinguish synthetic from human-labeled trajectories, but this does not validate the correctness of decisive-error labels, the causal claim that replacing the injected step flips failure to success, or the match to real-world failure distributions. The claim that synthetic labels are precise and realistic is therefore unsupported.

The method is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Section 3 says clustering generates one schema per cluster, but Algorithm 1 then loops over every annotated trajectory and inserts every generated schema. Key choices such as clustering method, thresholds, cache construction, schema filtering, schema distillation, and replay evaluation are not described sufficiently for reproduction.

Several headline claims are overstated. The framework is described as training-free and near-zero overhead, yet it requires labeled trajectories, GPT-5-generated schemas, embedding/retrieval infrastructure, and sometimes user feedback with ground-truth labels. The dynamic schema expansion/distillation mechanism is presented as part of the framework but is not clearly evaluated.

Baselines are inadequate for the strength of the claims. Fine-tuning is only briefly represented, apparently with one Qwen model, and stronger retrieval, summarization, RAG, verifier, or error-attribution baselines are missing. Naive ICL with full logs is a weak strawman given the paper’s own argument that full logs are too long and noisy.

Reported improvements are mixed despite claims of consistency. Some CORRECT rows are negative or marginal, e.g. Gemini-2.5-Flash Acc@1 on Algorithm-Generated decreases, and several exact-step accuracies remain very low on WHO&WHEN. The paper emphasizes tolerant Acc@k metrics that may substantially soften the difficulty of exact decisive-error localization.

The experimental reporting lacks statistical rigor. Although the paper says results are averaged over five runs, it provides no standard deviations, confidence intervals, significance tests, sample counts per condition, or clear train/schema/test split details.

Reproducibility is poor. The approach depends heavily on proprietary GPT-5/GPT-4o models and massive token generation, prompts are only partially provided, and the manuscript does not clearly state whether data, schemas, code, labels, and generated trajectories will be released.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. There are many formatting and grammar issues, unclear figure/table captions, cramped or malformed text, and contradictory statements such as claiming the oracle is superior while also saying CORRECT reaches 104% of oracle performance.

Limitations and ethics are insufficient. The paper does not seriously discuss risks from synthetic benchmark contamination, biased or unrealistic injected failures, privacy/security issues in multi-agent logs, dependence on proprietary LLMs, or failure modes where schema reuse could reinforce incorrect attributions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: decisive error localization in multi-agent LLM systems. The framing is useful, and the schema-cache idea is a plausible lightweight alternative to both zero-shot judging and costly fine-tuning.

CORRECT is simple, training-free, and practically motivated. Distilling recurring failure patterns into compact schemata and retrieving them at inference time is an intuitive design that fits the long, noisy trajectory setting well.

The empirical results show consistent relative gains across several model families and datasets. On WHO&WHEN, CORRECT improves exact-step accuracy for multiple backbones, and on CORRECT-Error it gives large gains under tolerant localization metrics.

The paper contributes a new large-scale benchmark, CORRECT-Error, and makes a serious attempt to validate synthetic error realism through human evaluation. This is valuable given the high cost and ambiguity of human annotation for multi-agent failures.
The presentation is mostly clear, with a readable method description, helpful figures, ablations over cache size and number of schemata, and prompt examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are not fully supported. Exact-step accuracy on the human-annotated WHO&WHEN benchmark remains quite low, e.g. 17.2% for GPT-5 + CORRECT on the human-crafted subset, so claims about substantially narrowing the gap to human-level error recognition feel overstated.

The benchmark validity is a central concern. CORRECT-Error is generated through GPT-based error injection and then evaluated with GPT-generated schemata, which risks circularity: the method may benefit from artifacts of the same synthetic generation process rather than genuinely natural MAS failures.

The human-alignment study shows that annotators struggle to distinguish synthetic from human errors, but this does not directly validate that the injected step is truly the decisive causal error under the paper's counterfactual definition. Realism of surface form is weaker evidence than correctness of localization labels.

Baselines are somewhat limited. Fine-tuning is only lightly explored, naive ICL is a weak retrieval baseline, and the paper does not compare against stronger compressed-retrieval, summarization, hierarchical tracing, or specialized attribution methods that could isolate whether the benefit comes from schemata specifically.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix includes prompts, but key details such as clustering procedure, thresholds, cache update settings, exact dataset construction protocol, train/test splits, sampling parameters, cost/runtime measurements, and code/data release status are insufficiently specified.

Some reported claims and wording are inconsistent or overconfident, such as “near-zero overhead” without a clear runtime table, “first” claims without careful qualification, and the oracle comparison statement that CORRECT reaches 104% of oracle performance. These presentation issues reduce trust in the empirical narrative.

Ethics and deployment limitations need a sharper treatment. Automated failure attribution in MAS could be used for monitoring and debugging, but also for unjustified replacement of expert diagnosis; the paper should more explicitly discuss misuse risks, uncertainty reporting, and safeguards for real deployments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: fine-grained decisive error localization in multi-agent LLM systems, where failures can propagate across agents and long trajectories make debugging costly.

The core idea of distilling prior failures into compact, reusable error schemata is practical and interpretable. It is a reasonable alternative to raw in-context examples, especially for long noisy trajectories.

The evaluation covers multiple model families and includes both an existing benchmark (WHO&WHEN) and a new synthetic benchmark. The paper also includes useful ablations on cache size, number of retrieved schemata, transfer, retrieval noise, and thresholds.

The manuscript is mostly well organized and includes prompts and implementation details in the appendix. The limitations section honestly discusses ambiguity in decisive-error labels and retrieval limitations.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is not fully convincing. On the human-crafted WHO&WHEN data, absolute exact-step accuracy remains very low even for the best model with CORRECT (17.2% Acc@0, 32.3% Acc@1), and several gains are small or negative on algorithm-generated data. This weakens claims of accurate and practical decisive error recognition.

The new CORRECT-Error benchmark is heavily synthetic and generated using LLMs plus schema-guided error injection, which risks circularity: the same kind of schema abstraction used to create failures may favor a schema-retrieval detector. Human judges being unable to distinguish synthetic from real trajectories does not establish that the injected decisive-error labels are causally correct or representative of real MAS failures.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract has a blank code URL, the dataset is only promised for release, sample sizes per dataset/table are unclear, clustering and schema-selection details are underspecified, and reliance on GPT-5/GPT-5-nano makes independent replication difficult.

The “training-free” and “near-zero overhead” framing is overstated. CORRECT still requires annotated trajectories, offline schema extraction, GPT-5-generated schemata, cache management, and in some settings billions of generation tokens for the benchmark. The reported overhead focuses on online prompt cost and does not account for the full pipeline.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness questions. The fine-tuning baseline appears limited to Qwen-2.5-7B and cross-split training, while CORRECT uses GPT-5-generated schemata; MIPRO and ICL details are sparse; and there is no strong retrieval/RAG baseline using summarized trajectories or human taxonomies.

Several claims are broader than the evidence supports, including scalability to millions of trajectories, adaptation to dynamic online deployments, and generalization across evolving real-world MAS. The online adaptation experiment is limited and does not clearly evaluate delayed/noisy feedback, label errors, or cache drift.

Presentation has some inconsistencies and rough edges: four vs five human labelers are both mentioned, the confusion-matrix interpretation is unclear, several figures/tables lack sample counts or uncertainty intervals, and statistical significance is not reported.

Ethics and limitations discussion is relatively shallow for a method that diagnoses failures in deployed agent systems. It does not sufficiently discuss privacy of cached trajectories/schemata, possible leakage of sensitive operational logs, or risks from automated misattribution leading to inappropriate agent updates.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: localizing decisive errors in multi-agent LLM systems is genuinely useful for debugging, monitoring, and recovery.

The central idea of caching compact, reusable error schemata is practical and intuitive, and the paper includes several relevant ablations on cache size, number of retrieved schemata, retrieval noise, transfer, and online adaptation.

The empirical section covers multiple model families and datasets, and the WHO&WHEN results suggest that schema guidance can improve over direct LLM-as-judge prompting on some real human/algorithm-labeled settings.
The authors acknowledge ambiguity in decisive-error labels and include a concrete failure case involving multi-error trajectories, which is helpful for understanding where the method breaks.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not strong enough to support the paper's broad claims. On the most credible existing benchmark, WHO&WHEN, exact-step accuracy remains very low: even GPT-5+CORRECT reaches only 17.2% on human-crafted examples, and several improvements are small or negative. This undermines claims of accurate decisive error recognition and practical reliability.

The new CORRECT-Error benchmark is heavily synthetic and appears circularly aligned with the proposed method. Errors are injected using GPT-based schema matching and generation, while CORRECT is evaluated by retrieving and applying schemata derived from similar labeled failures. This risks measuring recovery of the synthetic generation pattern rather than genuine error localization in natural MAS failures.

The human validation of CORRECT-Error is insufficient. Asking annotators whether trajectories look synthetic versus human-labeled does not validate that the injected decisive-error step is correct, unique, or useful. The manuscript also contains inconsistencies, e.g. it says four expert labelers but later reports statistics over five labelers.

The method is less novel than presented. It is essentially retrieval-augmented prompting with LLM-generated summaries/templates of past labeled failures. The paper claims 'first schema-guided detector' and strong originality, but does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from case-base reasoning, memory/RAG, exemplar compression, or prompt-template retrieval methods.

The 'training-free' and 'near-zero overhead' framing is misleading. The approach requires labeled trajectories to generate schemata, uses GPT-5 to create all schemata, reports over 3 billion tokens to synthesize the benchmark, and online cache expansion depends on user feedback or ground-truth labels. Offline and data-acquisition costs are substantial and not adequately accounted for.

The online adaptation mechanism is underspecified and partly circular: it adds new schemata when user feedback confirms successful recognition and can 'extract ground truth label from data', but real deployments often lack such labels. The fallback to LLM-as-judge confidence filtering is only discussed briefly and not convincingly evaluated.

Baselines are not fully convincing. Naive ICL with full trajectories is a weak strawman given known context-length issues; fine-tuning is only shown for Qwen-2.5-7B and cross-split settings; prompt optimization and retrieval baselines using summarized cases, taxonomies, or nearest compressed exemplars are missing.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is publicly available but the URL is blank in the manuscript. The experiments depend on proprietary or unreleased models such as GPT-5 and Gemini, and the dataset release is promised rather than demonstrated. Key implementation details for clustering, thresholds, splits, schema cache construction, and statistical uncertainty are incomplete.

Presentation quality is uneven, with formatting artifacts, cramped figures, missing URL, inconsistent terminology/capitalization, and overclaiming. Several claims such as 'cheap', 'scalable to millions', 'near-zero overhead', and 'faithfully reflects natural errors' are not supported by the provided evidence.

The impact/ethics discussion is superficial. The paper does not seriously discuss risks from mislocalizing blame to the wrong agent/component, privacy concerns in caching execution logs, or benchmark artifacts caused by synthetic GPT-generated failures.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: localizing the earliest decisive error in LLM-based multi-agent system trajectories. This is practically useful for debugging, monitoring, targeted restarts, and agent upgrades, and the motivation is well articulated with concrete evidence that existing LLM-as-judge methods perform poorly on long MAS traces.

The proposed CORRECT framework is simple but compelling: distill prior failures into compact error schemata, retrieve relevant schemata at inference time, and use them to guide diagnosis without fine-tuning. This is a pragmatic contribution that fits realistic online deployments better than repeatedly training specialized detectors.

The evaluation is broad in scope. The paper reports results on WHO&WHEN and the new CORRECT-Error benchmark, across multiple model families and datasets, with ablations on cache size, number of retrieved schemata, transfer, model upgrades, streaming-style adaptation, retrieval noise, and threshold sensitivity.

The empirical gains are meaningful. On WHO&WHEN, CORRECT improves exact-step accuracy for several models, including GPT-5 from 8.6% to 17.2% on the human-crafted split and from 18.3% to 38.1% on the algorithm-generated split. On CORRECT-Error, the reported average improvements are large, especially at tolerant accuracies.

The paper includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including prompts for schema generation and schema-guided detection, fine-tuning baseline hyperparameters, truncation robustness, and some failure case analysis. The limitations section is honest about subjectivity in decisive-error labels and weaknesses of semantic retrieval.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: CORRECT is essentially retrieval-augmented prompting over LLM-generated summaries/schemata of labeled failures. The framing is useful, but the paper could better distinguish the contribution from standard case-based reasoning, RAG, memory/caching, and prompt-template reuse for debugging agent traces.

The soundness of the strongest claims depends heavily on the synthetic CORRECT-Error benchmark. The benchmark is generated by GPT models from seeded human-labeled errors, and CORRECT itself uses GPT-generated schemata derived from labeled errors. This creates a risk that the method is especially well matched to the benchmark generation process. The human indistinguishability study helps, but it does not fully establish that performance transfers to naturally occurring deployment failures.

There are possible transductive-evaluation concerns. The paper says each trajectory is masked and cannot retrieve its own schema, but schemata are still generated from labeled trajectories in the same datasets and retrieved for test cases. This is a valid setting if framed as memory-based reuse with labeled historical failures, but it is less convincing as a clean generalization evaluation. More explicit train/validation/test splits, temporal splits, or leave-cluster/domain-out evaluation would strengthen the evidence.

Several reported accuracies remain low on the most realistic/human-crafted exact-step setting. For example, exact-step accuracy of 17.2% for GPT-5 + CORRECT on human-crafted WHO&WHEN is an improvement but still far from reliable decisive localization. The paper sometimes presents the method as enabling accurate diagnosis, while the absolute performance suggests it is better viewed as a useful aid than a dependable detector.

The human-alignment reporting is confusing and potentially inconsistent: the main text mentions four independent expert labelers, while the agreement statistic refers to “two out of five labelers.” The confusion-matrix interpretation is also not fully clear, e.g., 47.1% synthetic misclassified as human-labeled and 42.3% genuine correctly identified are not enough by themselves to prove realism without clearer class balance, task instructions, labeler expertise, and agreement statistics.

Baseline strength is mixed. The fine-tuning baseline appears weak and only uses Qwen-2.5-7B, while the strongest closed models are not fine-tuned or adapted. Naive ICL with full trajectories is a useful strawman, but stronger retrieval baselines using summarized exemplars, nearest-neighbor error reasons, human/LLM taxonomies, or trajectory chunk retrieval would be important to isolate whether “schema” structure is the key factor.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript claims public code availability but the visible URL is blank in the provided PDF, and the dataset release is phrased as future tense in places. Exact prompts are provided, but important details such as clustering choices, epsilon values, schema filtering/distillation procedures, schema cache construction, evaluation parsing, random seeds, and access to closed models may limit reproducibility.

The paper’s ethics/impact discussion is brief. It notes positive reliability benefits and no major negative impacts, but does not deeply discuss privacy risks in caching production trajectories, exposure of sensitive logs through schemata, model-generated diagnostic errors leading to incorrect interventions, or governance for user-feedback-derived labels. These are material concerns for the proposed online deployment setting.
